question: A property manager's primary responsibility to the property owner is best described as:
choice_a: Maximizing occupancy at any cost regardless of tenant quality
choice_b: Operating and maintaining the property to maximize its net income and preserve its value, consistent with the owner's instructions
choice_c: Minimizing all maintenance expenditures regardless of long-term impact on the property
choice_d: Setting rents independently of the owner's investment objectives
explanation: A property manager acts as the owner's agent, and the core duty is to run the property in a way that protects and grows the owner's investment while following the owner's stated goals. Chasing occupancy or cutting maintenance without regard to long-term value or the owner's wishes conflicts with that fiduciary role.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: In a percentage lease, commonly used for retail space, the tenant's total rent is typically structured as:
choice_a: A single flat amount that can never change for the entire lease term
choice_b: Rent calculated solely as a percentage of the landlord's operating expenses
choice_c: A base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales above a specified breakpoint
choice_d: Rent that increases only when the Consumer Price Index decreases
explanation: Percentage leases are common in retail settings and combine a guaranteed minimum (base) rent with an additional amount tied to the tenant's sales performance once sales exceed an agreed breakpoint. This aligns the landlord's return with the tenant's business success.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: Under a gross lease, which party is generally responsible for paying the property's operating expenses, such as taxes, insurance, and maintenance?
choice_a: The tenant
choice_b: The expenses are automatically split 50/50 by operation of law
choice_c: Neither party, since a gross lease waives all operating expenses
choice_d: The landlord
explanation: A gross lease bundles operating expenses into the rent the tenant pays, with the landlord remaining responsible for paying taxes, insurance, and maintenance out of that rent. This is common in residential and many office leases.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: A 'triple net' (NNN) lease requires the tenant to pay, in addition to base rent:
choice_a: Property taxes, insurance, and common area maintenance expenses
choice_b: Only the property taxes, with the landlord covering all other costs
choice_c: Only utility costs, with everything else covered by the landlord
choice_d: Nothing beyond the stated base rent amount
explanation: A triple net lease shifts the three major categories of operating costs -- taxes, insurance, and maintenance/CAM charges -- onto the tenant in addition to base rent. It is common in commercial and industrial leasing.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: A ground lease most commonly involves:
choice_a: A tenant leasing a fully constructed building for a short term of six months or less
choice_b: A tenant leasing the land only, typically for a long term, and constructing a building on it that the tenant owns during the lease period
choice_c: A landlord leasing furnished residential space on a month-to-month basis
choice_d: A lease that automatically transfers ownership of the land to the tenant upon signing
explanation: In a ground lease, the tenant leases the underlying land (often for 50 to 99 years) and typically constructs and owns improvements on it for the lease term, with the land and any improvements usually reverting to the landowner when the lease ends.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: As a general principle applicable across most residential leases, a landlord's security deposit is primarily intended to:
choice_a: Serve as an additional, non-refundable rent payment collected up front
choice_b: Automatically substitute for the tenant's last two months of rent
choice_c: Provide funds to cover unpaid rent or damage to the unit beyond normal wear and tear
choice_d: Cover the landlord's marketing costs for finding the next tenant
explanation: Security deposits generally exist to protect the landlord against a tenant's default on rent or against damage exceeding ordinary wear and tear, and are refundable to the extent not used for those purposes.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: The implied warranty of habitability generally obligates a residential landlord to:
choice_a: Provide luxury amenities regardless of what the lease specifies
choice_b: Guarantee the tenant will experience no inconvenience whatsoever during the tenancy
choice_c: Fully renovate the unit every year regardless of its condition
choice_d: Maintain the premises in a condition fit for human habitation, including essential services such as heat, water, and structural safety
explanation: Most jurisdictions imply a warranty of habitability into residential leases, requiring the landlord to keep the dwelling safe, sanitary, and fit to live in, covering things like working plumbing, heat, and structural integrity.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: The covenant of quiet enjoyment in a lease protects the tenant's right to:
choice_a: Possess and use the leased premises without unreasonable interference from the landlord
choice_b: Demand that the landlord lower the rent at any time during the lease
choice_c: Sublease the property without any restriction, regardless of the lease terms
choice_d: Terminate the lease without notice for any reason at all
explanation: Quiet enjoyment guarantees the tenant's right to possess and use the property without unreasonable disturbance from the landlord, such as improper entries or interference with utilities.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: When a property manager collects rents and pays expenses on behalf of an owner, the manager owes the owner a fiduciary duty best described as:
choice_a: Loyalty only to the tenants who occupy the property
choice_b: Loyalty and accurate accounting -- acting in the owner's best interest and maintaining honest records of all funds handled
choice_c: No fiduciary duty at all, since property management is considered purely ministerial
choice_d: Loyalty to whichever party happens to pay the higher fee
explanation: A property manager acting as the owner's agent owes fiduciary duties, including loyalty to the owner's interests and a duty to account accurately for all funds collected and disbursed on the owner's behalf.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: A property manager's fiduciary duty of reasonable care and skill requires the manager to:
choice_a: Personally perform every repair rather than hiring licensed contractors
choice_b: Guarantee that the property will never decline in value
choice_c: Exercise the degree of competence that a reasonably prudent property manager would use in operating and maintaining the property
choice_d: Disregard local building codes whenever the owner requests it
explanation: The duty of care requires a property manager to act with the competence and diligence a reasonably prudent manager would exercise, not to personally perform all tasks or guarantee outcomes.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), a property manager of a commercial property with public-facing common areas generally must:
choice_a: Comply only if the building was constructed after the year 2020
choice_b: Apply accessibility standards solely to individual residential units
choice_c: Ignore ADA requirements unless a specific tenant requests compliance
choice_d: Ensure reasonable accessibility of public and common areas for individuals with disabilities
explanation: The ADA requires places of public accommodation, including many commercial common areas managed for public use, to be reasonably accessible to individuals with disabilities, regardless of the building's construction date.
source_note: Federal Americans with Disabilities Act; PSI national content outline

question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act, a property manager advertising a residential rental unit must avoid:
choice_a: Any statement of preference, limitation, or discrimination based on a protected class
choice_b: Listing the square footage of the unit in the advertisement
choice_c: Mentioning the monthly rent amount in the advertisement
choice_d: Describing the unit's physical amenities, such as its appliances
explanation: The Fair Housing Act prohibits advertising that indicates a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, or disability. Neutral facts like size, rent, and amenities are not prohibited.
source_note: Federal Fair Housing Act; PSI national content outline

question: The key legal distinction between an assignment and a sublease is that in an assignment:
choice_a: The original tenant is automatically released from all liability under every circumstance
choice_b: The original tenant transfers the entire remaining lease term and privity of estate to the new party
choice_c: The landlord's consent is never required, regardless of the lease terms
choice_d: The new occupant must pay rent directly into a court-administered escrow
explanation: An assignment transfers the tenant's entire remaining interest in the lease to a new party, creating privity of estate between the landlord and the assignee, whereas a sublease transfers only part of the term and the original tenant remains directly liable to the landlord.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: A tenant who remains in possession after the lease term expires without the landlord's consent creates what is generally known as:
choice_a: A permanent life estate in the tenant's favor
choice_b: An automatic renewal for a full new term identical to the original lease
choice_c: A holdover tenancy, also called a tenancy at sufferance
choice_d: A joint tenancy between the landlord and the tenant
explanation: A tenant who stays past the lease term without the landlord's permission becomes a holdover tenant, also known as a tenant at sufferance, and the landlord may choose to evict or to treat the tenant as a periodic tenant.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: When a broker is engaged to help an owner set an appropriate asking rent for an investment property, the broker should primarily rely on:
choice_a: The owner's original purchase price for the property, regardless of current conditions
choice_b: The national average rent, regardless of the local market
choice_c: The single highest rent being charged anywhere in the state
choice_d: A market rent analysis comparing recent comparable rental listings and executed leases in the area
explanation: Setting a competitive, defensible rent -- a broker-level judgment task -- requires analyzing comparable rentals currently on the market and recently leased in the same submarket, similar to a sales CMA but for rental rates.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: setting rental rates)

question: In exercising professional judgment to recommend a lease rate for a broker's property management client, which of the following is LEAST relevant to the analysis?
choice_a: The tenant's personal preference for the unit's paint color scheme
choice_b: Current vacancy rates in the local rental submarket
choice_c: The operating expenses the owner needs the rent to cover
choice_d: Rental rates being achieved by comparable nearby properties
explanation: A cosmetic preference like paint color has no bearing on a defensible market rent recommendation, while vacancy trends, the owner's expense coverage needs, and comparable rents are all core inputs to that broker-level judgment.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: setting rental rates)

question: Under general landlord-tenant principles, responsibility for major structural repairs, such as a failing roof, typically falls on:
choice_a: The tenant, in every lease without exception
choice_b: The landlord, unless a specific lease provision shifts that obligation to the tenant
choice_c: Whichever party happens to discover the problem first
choice_d: The property's insurance carrier automatically, with no owner involvement required
explanation: Absent a lease clause allocating structural repair responsibility to the tenant, the landlord generally bears responsibility for major structural components, since these are typically outside a tenant's ordinary maintenance obligations.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: A written property management agreement between an owner and a broker should clearly define:
choice_a: A guarantee that the property will never experience a vacancy
choice_b: A waiver of the owner's right to ever review financial records
choice_c: The scope of the manager's authority, the term of the agreement, and the manager's compensation
choice_d: A requirement that the manager personally reside on the property
explanation: The management agreement is the source of the manager's authority and should spell out what the manager may do on the owner's behalf (leasing, maintenance decisions, spending limits), how long the agreement runs, and how the manager is compensated.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: property management agreements)

question: A property management agreement should also address termination provisions so that:
choice_a: The agreement can never be terminated by either party once it is signed
choice_b: Only the manager is permitted to terminate the agreement, never the owner
choice_c: Termination automatically forfeits any commissions the manager has already earned
choice_d: Both the owner and the manager understand how and under what conditions the agreement may be ended, such as by notice or for cause
explanation: Well-drafted management agreements specify termination rights and notice requirements for both parties, avoiding disputes over how and when the relationship can end.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: property management agreements)

question: An individual who manages rental property and collects rent for an owner in exchange for compensation generally must:
choice_a: Hold a real estate broker's license, or act as an agent under the supervision of a licensed broker
choice_b: Have no license of any kind, since property management is exempt from licensing in every state
choice_c: Hold only a notary commission
choice_d: Be a licensed attorney
explanation: Managing property and collecting rent for others for compensation is generally treated as a licensed real estate brokerage activity, requiring a broker's license or supervision by one, though specific exemptions vary by state.
source_note: hedge: general licensing principle, exact exemptions vary by state; national content outline

question: Rents and security deposits collected by a property manager on behalf of an owner must generally be:
choice_a: Deposited directly into the manager's personal checking account for convenience
choice_b: Deposited into a separate trust or escrow account, kept apart from the manager's personal or operating funds
choice_c: Converted to cash and kept in the property manager's office safe indefinitely
choice_d: Forwarded immediately into the tenant's own bank account
explanation: Client funds such as rents and security deposits must be held in a separate trust or escrow account rather than commingled with the manager's own operating or personal funds.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: trust accounts)

question: A property manager who uses funds from an owner's trust account to pay the manager's own personal expenses has committed:
choice_a: A routine and permissible bookkeeping adjustment
choice_b: A minor clerical error requiring no correction
choice_c: Conversion -- a serious breach of fiduciary duty involving misappropriation of client funds
choice_d: An action that is improper only if the owner happens to find out about it
explanation: Using trust account funds belonging to an owner or tenant for the manager's own purposes is conversion, one of the most serious fiduciary violations in property management.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: trust accounts)

question: As part of the fiduciary duty of accounting, a property manager is generally expected to:
choice_a: Provide financial reports to the owner only if the owner is formally subpoenaed
choice_b: Withhold all financial information from the owner in order to protect tenant privacy
choice_c: Report financial activity to the owner only once, at the very end of the management agreement
choice_d: Provide the owner with periodic financial reports summarizing rents collected, expenses paid, and account balances
explanation: The duty to account requires a property manager to keep accurate records and regularly report income, expenses, and account balances to the owner, not to withhold or delay that information.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: reports and disbursements)

question: When qualifying prospective tenants for a rental property, a property manager should:
choice_a: Apply the same objective screening criteria, such as income and credit standards, consistently to every applicant
choice_b: Apply stricter credit standards to applicants of a particular national origin
choice_c: Reject any applicant with children, regardless of the unit's size
choice_d: Vary the screening criteria from one applicant to the next at the manager's personal discretion
explanation: Uniform, objective, and consistently applied screening criteria let a manager properly qualify tenants financially while avoiding disparate treatment that could violate fair housing law.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: tenant procurement/qualification); Federal Fair Housing Act

question: Under the Fair Housing Act, a 'reasonable accommodation' for a tenant with a disability refers to:
choice_a: A physical alteration the tenant makes to the unit at the tenant's own expense
choice_b: A change in rules, policies, or services -- such as permitting an assistance animal despite a no-pets policy
choice_c: A requirement that the landlord waive all rent payments
choice_d: A benefit available only to tenants who have occupied the unit for at least five years
explanation: A reasonable accommodation is a change to a rule, policy, or service (such as waiving a no-pets policy for an assistance animal), distinct from a reasonable modification, which is a physical change to the premises.
source_note: Federal Fair Housing Act; PSI national content outline

question: Under the federal Fair Housing Act's familial status protections, a property manager generally may NOT:
choice_a: Verify an applicant's income or employment history
choice_b: Require every applicant to complete the same rental application
choice_c: Refuse to rent to a family because they have children, except in properties that qualify as housing for older persons
choice_d: Confirm that an applicant's income meets the property's stated rent-to-income ratio
explanation: Familial status is a protected class under the Fair Housing Act; refusing to rent to families with children is generally prohibited unless the property qualifies for the housing-for-older-persons exemption. Applying the same neutral financial screening to all applicants is permitted.
source_note: Federal Fair Housing Act; PSI national content outline

question: To terminate a month-to-month periodic tenancy under general landlord-tenant principles, a party generally must:
choice_a: Provide no notice at all, since periodic tenancies automatically end each month
choice_b: Obtain a court order before any notice may be given
choice_c: Wait until the tenant voluntarily agrees to leave, with no formal notice ever required
choice_d: Give the other party proper advance written notice, commonly around 30 days, before the desired termination date
explanation: Ending a periodic tenancy generally requires proper advance written notice of a legally required length, commonly around 30 days, rather than no notice or a court order as a precondition to giving notice.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle, exact notice periods vary by state (national content outline)

question: In many jurisdictions, if a landlord fails to make a necessary repair affecting habitability after proper notice, a residential tenant may be permitted to:
choice_a: Arrange for the repair and deduct a reasonable cost from future rent, subject to state law limits
choice_b: Stop paying rent permanently with no further obligation to the landlord
choice_c: Take possession of the landlord's other properties as compensation
choice_d: Automatically terminate the landlord's ownership of the property
explanation: Many states recognize a limited 'repair and deduct' remedy allowing a tenant to have a necessary habitability repair made and deduct a reasonable cost from rent, rather than a broader or unrelated remedy.
source_note: hedge: repair-and-deduct remedy exists in many but not all states; national content outline

question: Constructive eviction occurs when:
choice_a: A court formally orders the tenant removed for nonpayment of rent
choice_b: A landlord's actions or failure to act render the premises so unfit that the tenant is justified in vacating and terminating the lease
choice_c: A tenant is physically locked out of the unit by the landlord using self-help measures
choice_d: A tenant sublets the unit to another party without the landlord's permission
explanation: Constructive eviction arises when a landlord's substantial interference or failure to maintain the premises effectively forces the tenant out, justifying the tenant in treating the lease as terminated -- distinct from a formal court-ordered eviction or an illegal self-help lockout.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)

question: If a tenant abandons the leased premises before the lease term ends, most modern courts hold that the landlord:
choice_a: May let the unit sit vacant indefinitely and sue only at lease end for the entire remaining rent, with no obligation to attempt re-renting
choice_b: Automatically forfeits the right to collect any rent from that tenant
choice_c: Has a duty to make reasonable efforts to re-rent the unit (mitigate damages) rather than letting it sit vacant and billing the full remaining rent
choice_d: Must immediately sell the property to a new owner
explanation: The modern majority rule imposes a duty on the landlord to mitigate damages by making reasonable efforts to re-rent an abandoned unit, rather than allowing damages to accrue unchecked.
source_note: hedge: majority modern rule; some jurisdictions differ (national content outline)

question: Under general landlord-tenant principles, a landlord's right to enter an occupied rental unit for a non-emergency purpose, such as an inspection or repair, typically requires:
choice_a: No notice of any kind, since the landlord owns the property
choice_b: The tenant's notarized written consent obtained separately before every single entry
choice_c: A court order for any entry, regardless of the purpose
choice_d: Reasonable advance notice to the tenant, consistent with the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment
explanation: Landlords generally must give reasonable advance notice before entering an occupied unit for routine, non-emergency purposes, balancing the landlord's access needs against the tenant's right to quiet enjoyment.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle, exact notice periods vary by state (national content outline)

question: In a commercial triple net lease, a 'CAM reconciliation' refers to the process by which:
choice_a: The landlord compares the tenant's estimated common area maintenance payments made during the year to the actual CAM expenses incurred, then bills or credits the difference
choice_b: The tenant recalculates the landlord's mortgage payment
choice_c: The landlord permanently waives all common area maintenance charges
choice_d: The tenant takes over ownership of the property's common areas
explanation: CAM reconciliation true-ups the tenant's estimated common area maintenance payments against actual expenses for the period, resulting in an additional bill or a credit for the difference.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: A lease provision that periodically increases rent based on changes in the Consumer Price Index is known as a:
choice_a: Percentage lease clause
choice_b: CPI-based (cost-of-living) escalation clause
choice_c: Graduated ground lease clause
choice_d: Habitability clause
explanation: A CPI-based escalation clause ties periodic rent increases to changes in a published cost-of-living index, distinct from a percentage lease, which ties rent to a tenant's gross sales.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: A lease clause giving the tenant the right, but not the obligation, to extend the lease for an additional term under specified conditions is called a:
choice_a: Right of first refusal to purchase the property
choice_b: Estoppel certificate
choice_c: Renewal (extension) option
choice_d: Subordination clause
explanation: A renewal or extension option gives the tenant the choice to extend the lease term on agreed conditions, which is distinct from a purchase right of first refusal, an estoppel certificate confirming lease facts, or a subordination clause addressing lien priority.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management

question: As part of sound risk management, a property manager should generally:
choice_a: Avoid documenting the property's condition in order to reduce paperwork
choice_b: Cancel the owner's insurance policy once tenants move in, to save money
choice_c: Rely solely on tenants' personal insurance policies to cover the building itself
choice_d: Ensure adequate property and liability insurance is maintained and document unit condition through move-in and move-out inspections
explanation: Maintaining adequate insurance coverage and documenting unit condition at move-in and move-out are basic risk-management practices that protect the owner and limit disputes over damage.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: risk management)

question: Before authorizing a major capital improvement to the property, such as a full roof replacement, a property manager should generally:
choice_a: Obtain the owner's approval, consistent with the scope of authority granted in the management agreement
choice_b: Proceed without informing the owner, since the manager is presumed to have unlimited spending authority
choice_c: Use funds from the tenants' security deposit trust account to pay for it
choice_d: Delay the project indefinitely without ever consulting the owner
explanation: Major capital expenditures generally exceed a manager's routine authority and should be approved by the owner in line with the management agreement, and must never be funded from tenant trust deposits.
source_note: PSI national content outline: Leasing & Property Management (broker-level: maintenance and improvements)

question: Under federal law, a landlord leasing residential housing built before 1978 must generally:
choice_a: Fully remove all paint from the building before any tenant moves in
choice_b: Disclose known information about lead-based paint hazards and provide the tenant an EPA-approved information pamphlet on lead hazards
choice_c: Provide the disclosure only for buildings built after the year 2000
choice_d: Provide the disclosure only if the tenant is a family with children
explanation: Federal law requires landlords of pre-1978 housing to disclose known lead-based paint hazards and provide tenants an EPA-approved pamphlet, regardless of whether the tenant has children.
source_note: Federal Residential Lead-Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act (Title X); PSI national content outline

question: If a residential tenant fails to pay rent, a landlord generally must:
choice_a: Immediately change the locks and remove the tenant's belongings without any court involvement
choice_b: Shut off the unit's utilities to pressure the tenant into leaving
choice_c: Pursue the legal eviction process through the courts rather than resorting to self-help measures such as changing the locks or removing the tenant's belongings
choice_d: Physically remove the tenant without any legal process
explanation: Self-help evictions -- such as lockouts, utility shutoffs, or forcibly removing a tenant -- are generally illegal; a landlord must use the judicial eviction (unlawful detainer) process instead.
source_note: hedge: standard real estate principle (national content outline)
